Modeling bots on `User` means bots reuse existing `Membership`, `Room`, `Message` (`creator_id` FK to `users`), `User::Avatar`, `Message::Broadcasts`, and `Room::MessagePusher` pipelines without polymorphism or schema duplication: - **Open rooms**: `User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (`after_create_commit`) and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users` include active bots automatically. - **Closed & direct rooms**: `Rooms::ClosedsController`, `Rooms::DirectsController`, and `Autocompletable::UsersController` query `User.active`, allowing bots to be added to rooms the same way as people. - **Human-only surfaces**: `User.without_bots` excludes bots from the `/account/edit` member management list, session login/transfer, IP bans, and direct-message sidebar placeholders. - **Soft deletion**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, setting `status: :deactivated`, clearing `bot_token: nil`, and removing non-direct room memberships while keeping historical messages authored by the bot intact. ### Ownership & Authorization - Any signed-in member can access `/bots`, `/bots/new`, and `POST /bots`. - `/bots` (`BotsController#index`) lists `Current.user.bots.active` for regular members and `User.active_bots` for administrators on a single page without pagination, with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `turbo-cache-control: no-store`. - `User::Role#can_administer?(record)` returns `false` for bots themselves, `true` for administrators, and `true` when `self == record&.creator`, authorizing `edit`, `update`, and `destroy` on `BotsController`. ### Bot Code & HTTP Messaging API - **Bot code format**: `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"` (`User#bot_key`). `User.authenticate_bot` verifies numeric `id`, active bot status, and compares the full `bot_key` via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`. - **Log hygiene**: `:bot_code` (alongside `:token` and `:_key`) is filtered in `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb`. - **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`Bots::MessagesController#create`). - Inherits from `ActionController::Base` (including `ActiveStorage::SetCurrent`, `BlockBannedRequests`, `SetCurrentRequest`, `VersionHeaders`) so CLI User-Agents are never blocked by browser version gates. - Overrides `self.dispatch` for non-multipart requests to set `action_dispatch.request.request_parameters = {}` so raw shell payloads sent via `curl -d "..."` (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) containing `%`, `&`, or arbitrary bytes never trigger `ActionController::BadRequest` before reaching the action, and raw message text is kept out of parameter logs. - Reads `request.raw_post` as UTF-8, HTML-escapes text, converts newlines to `
`, and creates the message via `@room.messages.create_with_attachment!`. - Responds `401 Unauthorized` (invalid/revoked bot code, checked before room lookup to avoid room ID enumeration), `404 Not Found` (unknown room or bot not a member of the room), `422 Unprocessable Content` (blank body and no attachment, enforced by `Message#ensure_has_content`), or `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`. ### Notes for Future Extensions - **`Location: /messages/:message_id`**: Returning `/messages/:message_id` provides a canonical message identifier that future bot endpoints (e.g., bot message updates, deletions, or file/attachment endpoints) can target while verifying `message.creator == authenticated_bot`. - **Attachments**: `Message#ensure_has_content` and `Bots::MessagesController#message_params` already coordinate with `Message::Attachment` (`create_with_attachment!`), making dedicated multipart or binary file-upload extensions straightforward. require "surfguard"

module RestrictedHTTP
  class Violation < StandardError; end

  # The address policy lives in the surfguard gem so this app, Basecamp, HEY and
  # Fizzy classify "internal" the same way instead of each keeping a copy that
  # drifts. The callers here hand a bare hostname in and pin the address that
  # comes back, so this stays a hostname-in, address-out shim.
  module PrivateNetworkGuard
    extend self

    # A hostname that resolves to nothing (NXDOMAIN, timeout, empty answer)
    # raises Surfguard::Unresolvable, which we let propagate as a lookup failure
    # -- the same way the old Resolv.getaddress guard raised Resolv::ResolvError,
    # and the callers here already treat it as a fetch failure. The Violation is
    # reserved for a host that resolves to a blocked address (an empty list back
    # from resolve_public_ips), so a transient DNS miss is never misreported as
    # an SSRF attempt.
    def resolve(hostname)
      Surfguard.resolve_public_ips(hostname).first or
        raise Violation.new("Attempt to access private IP via #{hostname}")
    end

    def private_ip?(ip)
      Surfguard.blocked_address?(ip)
    end
  end
end

class WebPush::Pool
  attr_reader :delivery_pool, :invalidation_pool, :connection, :invalid_subscription_handler

  def initialize(invalid_subscription_handler:)
    @delivery_pool = Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor.new(max_threads: 50, queue_size: 10000)
    @invalidation_pool = Concurrent::FixedThreadPool.new(1)
    @connection = Net::HTTP::Persistent.new(name: "web_push", pool_size: 150)
    @invalid_subscription_handler = invalid_subscription_handler
  end

  def queue(payload, subscriptions)
    subscriptions.find_each do |subscription|
      deliver_later(payload, subscription)
    end
  end

  def shutdown
    connection.shutdown
    shutdown_pool(delivery_pool)
    shutdown_pool(invalidation_pool)
  end

  private
    def deliver_later(payload, subscription)
      # Ensure any AR operations happen before we post to the thread pool
      notification = subscription.notification(**payload)
      subscription_id = subscription.id

      delivery_pool.post do
        deliver(notification, subscription_id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.deliver: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    rescue Concurrent::RejectedExecutionError
    end

    def deliver(notification, id)
      notification.deliver(connection: connection)
    rescue WebPush::ExpiredSubscription, OpenSSL::OpenSSLError => ex
      invalidate_subscription_later(id) if invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    def invalidate_subscription_later(id)
      invalidation_pool.post do
        invalid_subscription_handler.call(id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.invalid_subscription_handler: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    end

    def shutdown_pool(pool)
      pool.shutdown
      pool.kill unless pool.wait_for_termination(1)
    end
end

  "output_head": "class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end
end
class Room::MessagePusher
  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(mentionees)
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)
    end

    def relevant_subscriptions
      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)
    end
end
# Rooms where only a subset of all users on the account have been explicited granted membership.
class Rooms::Closed < Room
end
# Rooms for direct message chats between users. These act as a singleton, so a single set of users will
# always refer to the same direct room.
class Rooms::Direct < Room
  class << self
    def find_or_create_for(users)
      find_for(users) || create_for({}, users: users)
    end

    private
      # FIXME: Find a more performant algorithm that won't be a problem on accounts with 10K+ direct rooms,
      # which could be to store the membership id list as a hash on the room, and use that for lookup.
      def find_for(users)
        all.joins(:users).detect do |room|
          Set.new(room.user_ids) == Set.new(users.pluck(:id))
        end
      end
  end

  def default_involvement
    "everything"
  end
end

class Opengraph::Metadata
  include ActiveModel::Model
  include ActiveModel::Validations::Callbacks
  include ActionView::Helpers::SanitizeHelper

  include Fetching

  ATTRIBUTES = %i[ title url image description ]
  attr_accessor *ATTRIBUTES

  before_validation :sanitize_fields

  validates_presence_of :title, :url, :description
  validate :ensure_valid_image_url

  private
    def sanitize_fields
      self.title = sanitize(strip_tags(title))
      self.description = sanitize(strip_tags(description))
    end

    def ensure_valid_image_url
      if image.present?
        errors.add :image, "url is invalid" unless Opengraph::Location.new(image).valid?
      end
    end
end
module Opengraph::Metadata::Fetching
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  module ClassMethods
    def from_url(url)
      document = fetch_document(url)
      attributes = document.opengraph_attributes
      new attributes.merge(url: valid_canonical_url(attributes[:url], url), image: valid_image_content_type(attributes[:image]))
    end

    private
      TWITTER_HOSTS = %w[ twitter.com www.twitter.com x.com www.x.com ]
      FX_TWITTER_HOST = "fxtwitter.com"
      ALLOWED_IMAGE_CONTENT_TYPES = %w[ image/jpeg image/png image/gif image/webp ]

      def fetch_document(untrusted_url)
        tweet_url?(untrusted_url) ? fetch_fxtwitter_document(untrusted_url) : fetch_non_fxtwitter_document(untrusted_url)
      end

      def fetch_fxtwitter_document(untrusted_url)
        fxtwitter_url = replace_twitter_domain_for_opengraph_support(untrusted_url)

        Opengraph::Location.new(fxtwitter_url).then do |location|
          # fxtwitter.com HTML response does not include character encoding, resulting in emojis and quotes not
          # being encoded properly.
          Opengraph::Document.new(location.read_html.force_encoding("UTF-8"))
        end
      end

      def fetch_non_fxtwitter_document(untrusted_url)
        Opengraph::Location.new(untrusted_url).then do |location|
          Opengraph::Document.new(location.read_html)
        end
      end

      def valid_canonical_url(url, fallback)
        Opengraph::Location.new(url).valid? ? url : fallback
      end

      def valid_image_content_type(image)

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end

      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)

class Room::MessagePusher
  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(mentionees)
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)
    end

    def relevant_subscriptions
      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)
    end

  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

    end

require "mocha/minitest"
require "webmock/minitest"
require "turbo/broadcastable/test_helper"

WebMock.enable!

class ActiveSupport::TestCase
  include ActiveJob::TestHelper

  parallelize(workers: :number_of_processors)

  # Setup all fixtures in test/fixtures/*.yml for all tests in alphabetical order.
  fixtures :all

  include SessionTestHelper, MentionTestHelper, TurboTestHelper, NetworkTestHelper

  setup do
    ActionCable.server.pubsub.clear

    Rails.configuration.tap do |config|
      config.x.web_push_pool.shutdown
      config.x.web_push_pool = WebPush::Pool.new \
        invalid_subscription_handler: config.x.web_push_pool.invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    WebMock.disable_net_connect!
  end

  teardown do
    WebMock.reset!
  end
end

  def applicable?
    normalize_tweet_url(solo_unfurled_url) == normalize_tweet_url(content.to_plain_text)
  end

    fragment.replace("div") { |node| node.tap { |n| n.inner_html = unfurled_links.first.to_s } }
  end

  private
    TWITTER_DOMAINS = %w[ x.com twitter.com ]
    TWITTER_DOMAIN_MAPPING = { "x.com" => "twitter.com" }

      unfurled_links.first["href"] if unfurled_links.size == 1

      end.to_s

      url.present? && TWITTER_DOMAINS.any? { |domain| url.strip.include?(domain) }

class ContentFilters::SanitizeAttributes < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  # Runs after SanitizeTags, so passing the same allowed tags makes the tag pass
  # a no-op and only attributes are scrubbed.
  def apply
    sanitizer.sanitize fragment.to_html, tags: allowed_tags, attributes: allowed_attributes
  end

  private
    # Presentation styling relies on class attributes (e.g. unfurled link embeds),
    # which the standard ActionText set doesn't include.

    # scrubber isolated.

      sanitizer_class.new
    end

      ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer.class
    end

      ContentFilters::SanitizeTags::ALLOWED_TAGS
    end

    def allowed_attributes
      standard_allowed_attributes + EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES
    end

    # exposed at the module level.
    def standard_allowed_attributes
      ActionText::ContentHelper.allowed_attributes ||
        (sanitizer_class.allowed_attributes + ActionText::Attachment::ATTRIBUTES).to_a
    end

## Self-hosting Campfire

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional, single-machine deployment.
This includes the web app, background jobs, caching, file serving, and SSL.

> [!TIP]
> The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once), which handles installation, updates, and backups for you. See the [README](../README.md#deploying-with-once) for details. This guide covers running the Docker image by hand.

We recommend using `ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, which always points to the most recent tagged release - the most stable and battle-tested version of Campfire.

We provide a tagged release for every major, minor and patch version of Campfire, so you can also pin your deployment to a specific version if you want to avoid unexpected changes. For example:

```bash
# exactly version 1.4.4
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1.4.4

# any 1.4.x version
# e.g. 1.4.4 or 1.4.5
# the last number is usually changed for bug fixes
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1.4

# any 1.x version
# e.g. 1.4.4 or 1.5.0
# the middle number is usually changed for changes to, or addition of, features
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1
```

If you want to live on the bleeding edge, the `main` tag tracks the main release branch instead.
It changes with every merged pull request, so it's the newest - but least battle-tested - version of Campfire.

To run it you'll need three things:
1. a machine that runs Docker
2. a mounted volume (so that your database and file attachments are kept around between restarts)
3. some environment variables for configuration

If you'd rather build the image yourself from your own copy of the source, you can do that too:

```sh
docker build -t campfire .
```

### Mounting a storage volume

Campfire keeps all of its storage - the database and uploaded file attachments - inside the path `/rails/storage`.
By default Docker containers don't persist storage between runs, so you'll want to mount a persistent volume into that location.

The simplest way to do this is with the `--volume` flag with `docker run`. For example:

```sh
docker run --volume campfire:/rails/storage ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

That will create a named volume (called `campfire`) and mount it into the correct path.
Docker will manage where that volume is actually stored on your server.

You can also specify the data location yourself, mount a network drive, and more.
Check the Docker documentation to find out more about what's available.

### Configuring with environment variables

To configure your Campfire installation, you can use environment variables.
At a minimum you'll want to configure your secret key and your SSL domain.

#### Secrets

Campfire needs a few secret values that are specific to your instance:

- `SECRET_KEY_BASE` - the basis for cryptographic features like signed cookies. This should be a long, unguessable random string.
- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`/`VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` - a key pair used for sending Web Push notifications.

You can generate them by running:

```sh
docker run --rm ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest script/admin/generate-secrets
```

It prints a fresh set of values ready to set as environment variables:

```
SECRET_KEY_BASE=...
VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=...
VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=...
```

Keep them safe and reuse the same values across restarts and upgrades - changing them later will invalidate sessions and push notification subscriptions.

#### SSL

If you want the Campfire container to handle its own SSL (HTTPS) automatically (via Let's Encrypt), you just need to specify the domain name that you're running it on.
You can do that with the `TLS_DOMAIN` environment variable.

> [!NOTE]
> If you're using SSL, you'll want to allow traffic on ports 80 and 443.

So if you were running on `chat.example.com` you could enable SSL like this:

```sh
docker run --publish 80:80 --publish 443:443 --env TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com ...
```

If you are terminating SSL in some other proxy in front of Campfire, or aren't using SSL at all (for example, if you want to run it locally on your laptop), then you should set `DISABLE_SSL=true` instead and just publish port 80:

```sh
docker run --publish 80:80 --env DISABLE_SSL=true ...
```

#### Error reporting (optional)

To enable error reporting to Sentry in production, supply your DSN in the `SENTRY_DSN` environment variable.
To disable Sentry initialization entirely, set `SKIP_TELEMETRY=true`.

### Example

Putting it all together, here's a complete `docker run` invocation:

```sh
docker run \
  --name campfire \
  --publish 80:80 --publish 443:443 \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --env SECRET_KEY_BASE=$YOUR_SECRET_KEY_BASE \
  --env VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=$YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY \
  --env VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=$YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY \
  --env TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

And here's an equivalent `docker-compose.yml` that you could use to run Campfire via `docker compose up`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    environment:
      - SECRET_KEY_BASE=abcdefabcdef
      - TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com
      - VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=myvapidprivatekey
      - VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=myvapidpublickey
    volumes:
      - campfire:/rails/storage

volumes:
  campfire:
```

### First run

When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through creating an admin account.

> [!TIP]
> The email address of this admin account will be shown on the login page so that people who forget their password know who to contact for help.
> (You can change this email later in the settings.)

Campfire is single-tenant: any rooms designated "public" will be accessible by all users in the system.
To support entirely distinct groups of customers, you would deploy multiple instances of the application.

### Upgrading

All of Campfire's state lives in the mounted volume, so upgrading is a matter of pulling a newer image and recreating the container:

```sh
docker pull ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

Any pending database migrations run automatically when the container boots.

### Backups

To back up your instance, back up the contents of the `/rails/storage` volume.

Because the SQLite database may be written to at any moment, you shouldn't copy its files directly while Campfire is running.
Instead, first run `script/admin/prepare-backup` inside the running container to produce a consistent snapshot of the database (it's written to `storage/backups/` inside the volume):

```sh
docker exec campfire script/admin/prepare-backup
```

(If you're using Docker Compose, replace `docker exec campfire` with `docker compose exec web`)

Then archive the whole storage volume to a file on the host:

```sh
docker run --rm \
  --user root \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --volume "$PWD":/backup \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest \
  tar czf "/backup/campfire-backup.tar.gz" -C /rails storage
```

This gives you a `campfire-backup.tar.gz` in your current directory containing the database snapshot and all uploaded files.
Copy it somewhere safe, ideally off the machine.

To restore, extract the archive back into a (stopped) instance's volume, and replace the live database with the snapshot:

```sh
docker run --rm \
  --user root \
  --volume campfire:/rails/storage \
  --volume "$PWD":/backup \
  ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest \
  bash -c "tar xzf /backup/campfire-backup.tar.gz -C /rails &&
           cp /rails/storage/backups/production.sqlite3 /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3 &&
           rm -f /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3-wal /rails/storage/db/production.sqlite3-shm &&
           chown -R rails:rails /rails/storage"
```

Then start Campfire again.

**Deep Dive into the Bot Webhook Implementation**

Okay, so the task at hand is crystal clear – we're adding webhook functionality to our Campfire bot integration. Before I dive into any code, I need to methodically break down *every* requirement. Let's make sure we are not making any assumptions, and that we have a solid understanding of all the constraints.

First, let's establish the context: We're extending an existing Rails chat application, and the QA automation is critical, which means we MUST adhere to the specified labels and UI conventions (checkboxes for switches, native `confirm()` dialogs).

The core of the new feature involves allowing bot authors to configure a webhook URL. This webhook will be triggered when a user mentions the bot in a message. The data structure is precisely defined – a JSON payload with an "event" type "mention", author details, room information (including the bot's own posting URL, very important), and the message content (stripped of the bot mention). The bot can respond with either a `200` (text/plain or text/html) to post a message, or a `204` to post nothing. The response must be *synchronous*, not asynchronous.

This means the application needs to handle the following:

1.  **Bot Form Update:** Add a "Webhook URL" field to both the new bot form and the edit bot form.
2.  **Webhook Trigger:** Detect when a bot is mentioned in a message and then trigger the webhook. The data to send to the webhook is precisely described in the document.
3.  **Webhook Response Handling:** Parse the bot's response and, based on the status code, post the response or take no action.
4.  **Error Handling:** Ensure that webhook calls do not slow down the user experience. This means the call has to be asynchronous.

Since we are extending an existing application, the starting point is critical:

First, let's explore how bots are currently modeled in the database. I'll need to check the database schema (`db/schema.rb`) and migration files (specifically, `db/migrate/20251213000000_add_bots_to_users.rb`) to understand the existing data model, particularly how "bots" are represented. Does an existing `webhooks` table exist? Or could the `webhook_url` fit in the existing `users` table, or should a new table be made for `Webhook`? I'll perform a quick search of the codebase for existing references to "webhook" to see if there are any existing implementations that we can reuse or leverage.

**Deep Dive into Webhook Implementation**

Alright, let's break this down systematically. The initial goal is clear: implement an optional webhook URL for bots within the existing system. The visual cue of a globe icon, perfectly matched in size to other icons, confirms this aligns with the current design conventions.

My first thought is around data storage. Should this be a separate `webhooks` table or a `webhook_url` column directly on the `users` table, or on a `Webhook` model with a virtual attribute? I need to analyze both options critically, considering the existing structure (like how bots are already modeled in the codebase). Thinking about the form handling, the existing `form_with` approach in `app/views/bots/_form.html.erb` seems to support direct field integration (e.g., `form.text_field :name`) if we add a `webhook_url` attribute to the `bot` object. That would be easier than an association.

Key to this decision is the "removes the bot's webhook" part of the prompt. This implies that setting an empty URL should *delete* the webhook. This is significant. If we go with a `webhooks` table, then saving an empty URL would trigger a `webhook&.destroy`. Alternatively, if we store the webhook URL directly on the user model, a simple `webhook_url = nil` would handle the removal.

Next, I need to consider all related aspects. When a bot is deactivated, what should happen to its webhook? It must be removed or deactivated to prevent unwanted calls. If a bot is deleted/deactivated, its `bot_token` is cleared to `nil`, its memberships in non-direct rooms are deleted. We need to do the same for the webhook: ensure it's not triggered after deactivation.

I must also check and ensure whether we are filtering sensitive parameters in logs. I'll need to check if the filtering includes `webhook_url`, or if we need to configure this. Filtering is relevant only for logging, and should not impact the params.

Then, there's a detailed comparison between two main options. A dedicated `Webhook` model (`webhooks` table) offers a clean domain object to encapsulate URL validation, payload generation, and HTTP delivery via a `deliver` method, or `deliver_later` via a job. However, we could achieve the same with a `webhook_url` column on `users`. It is easier to implement via a column on the `users` table (since it is an attribute for the bot). With a column on `users`, we can STILL build a `Bot::Webhook` or `User::Bot::Webhook` for a PORO/concern that handles the domain-related functionality.

Important: form validation! If saving the form fails, we need to ensure the webhook URL field retains its value, preventing data loss. Both scenarios, new bot creation and editing an existing one, need to be considered. Both of them will be handled cleanly with the column approach!

Finally, the prompt specifies "optional" and "a bot may have one". We don't have a requirement for multiple webhooks per bot. Using a column on `users` with validation, and an optional `Bot::Webhook` class, simplifies the implementation and keeps it clean. There's no major disadvantage to this approach compared to using a `webhooks` table, since the logic can be cleanly encapsulated in the `User::Bot::Webhook` class. messages.thinking:
**Webhook URL Validation and SSRF/Localhost Considerations**

Okay, the migration for the webhook URL is straightforward, that's good. But now, let's think critically about URL validation and the potential for Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), especially in our QA tests. This is where things get interesting.

I need to figure out how the QA tests will actually *test* the webhooks. The tests run within this container, or a test runner container simulating a headless browser, which means the test *needs* to spin up its own local HTTP server. I can see it now: `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/webhook`, `http://localhost:<port>/webhook`, even `http://[::1]:<port>/...`, or container-specific addresses. The QA test will fill the bot's webhook URL with one of those, save the bot, send a message that triggers the bot, and then assert that the local server *actually* receives the POST request. This is a crucial, vital point, now that I have it so clear in my mind.

Here's the problem: if we use `RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard` (like Surfguard) unconditionally, we're blocking `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `::1`, and all the private network ranges! That kills the QA tests *and* self-hosted deployments using Docker Compose, where bots regularly interact with services on those very networks. My brain is going a million miles a minute here. If we use a restrictive URL validator, we're hosing our QA, and breaking self-hosting!

Let's look at how Campfire, in its self-hosted form, handles bot webhooks. How should we validate the `webhook_url`? First, if it's blank (`nil` or `""`), it's valid: webhooks are *optional*. If it's present, it MUST be a valid HTTP or HTTPS URL, meaning `URI::HTTP` (HTTP or HTTPS) with a non-blank `host`. I need to ensure a valid URL!

I should use Ruby's `URI.parse` and check `uri.is_a?(URI::HTTP) && uri.host.present?`. This will return `true` for a valid URL and `false` for an invalid one. This approach will catch everything, so long as the bot has a valid HTTP URL. I can also use it to validate the input to `<input type="url">`, and if a person bypasses that, the server side validation can reject an invalid URL. I'm imagining a server-side validation on `User::Bot` that cleanly returns a `422 Unprocessable Content` if the URL is invalid.

I'm thinking, in a self-hosted environment, bots could run on `localhost` or Docker bridge networks or internal VPCs. Both the QA and real bots *need* to allow those addresses, so we must *NOT* block localhost or private network IPs. I'm going to quickly check if DNS even works in this container just to be sure... and then I'll finalize the new validation strategy.

    else
      room.name
    end
  end

  private
    def composer_data_options(room)
      {
        controller: "composer drop-target",
        action: composer_data_actions,
        composer_messages_outlet: "#message-area",
        composer_toolbar_class: "composer--rich-text", composer_room_id_value: room.id
      }
    end

    def composer_data_actions
      drag_and_drop_actions = "drop-target:drop@window->composer#dropFiles"

      trix_attachment_actions =
        "trix-file-accept->composer#preventAttachment refresh-room:online@window->composer#online"

      remaining_actions =
        "typing-notifications#stop paste->composer#pasteFiles turbo:submit-end->composer#submitEnd refresh-room:offline@window->composer#offline"

      [ drop_target_actions, drag_and_drop_actions, trix_attachment_actions, remaining_actions ].join(" ")
    end
end

module ActionText
  module PlainTextConversion
    extend self

    def node_to_plain_text(node)
      BottomUpReducer.new(node).reduce do |n, child_values|
        plain_text_for_node(n, child_values)
      end.then(&method(:remove_trailing_newlines))
    end

    private
      def plain_text_for_node(node, child_values)
        if respond_to?(plain_text_method_for_node(node), true)
          send(plain_text_method_for_node(node), node, child_values)
        else
          plain_text_for_child_values(child_values)
        end
      end

      def plain_text_method_for_node(node)
        :"plain_text_for_#{node.name}_node"
      end

      def plain_text_for_child_values(child_values)
        child_values.join
      end

      def plain_text_for_unsupported_node(node, _child_values)
        ""
      end

      %i[ script style].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_unsupported_node
      end

      def plain_text_for_block(node, child_values)
        "#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}\n\n"
      end

      %i[ h1 p ].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_block
      end

      def plain_text_for_list(node, child_values)
        "#{break_if_nested_list(node, plain_text_for_block(node, child_values))}"
      end

      %i[ ul ol ].each do |element|
        alias_method :"plain_text_for_#{element}_node", :plain_text_for_list
      end

      def plain_text_for_br_node(node, _child_values)
        "\n"
      end

      def plain_text_for_text_node(node, _child_values)
        remove_trailing_newlines(node.text)
      end

      def plain_text_for_div_node(node, child_values)
        "#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}\n"
      end

      def plain_text_for_figcaption_node(node, child_values)
        "[#{remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))}]"
      end

      def plain_text_for_blockquote_node(node, child_values)
        text = plain_text_for_block(node, child_values)
        return "“”" if text.blank?

        text = text.dup
        text.insert(text.rindex(/\S/) + 1, "”")
        text.insert(text.index(/\S/), "“")
        text
      end

      def plain_text_for_li_node(node, child_values)
        bullet = bullet_for_li_node(node)
        text = remove_trailing_newlines(plain_text_for_child_values(child_values))
        indentation = indentation_for_li_node(node)

        "#{indentation}#{bullet} #{text}\n"
      end

      def remove_trailing_newlines(text)
        text.chomp("")
      end

      def bullet_for_li_node(node)
        if list_node_name_for_li_node(node) == "ol"
          index = node.parent.elements.index(node)
          "#{index + 1}."
        else
          "•"
        end
      end

      def list_node_name_for_li_node(node)
        node.ancestors.lazy.map(&:name).grep(/^[uo]l$/).first
      end

      def indentation_for_li_node(node)
        depth = list_node_depth_for_node(node)
        if depth > 1
          "  " * (depth - 1)
        end
      end

      def list_node_depth_for_node(node)
        node.ancestors.map(&:name).grep(/^[uo]l$/).count
      end

      def break_if_nested_list(node, text)
        if list_node_depth_for_node(node) > 0
          "\n#{text}"
        else
          text
        end
      end

      class BottomUpReducer # :nodoc:
        def initialize(node)
          @node = node
          @values = {}
        end

        def reduce(&block)
          traverse_bottom_up(@node) do |n|
            child_values = @values.values_at(*n.children)
            @values[n] = block.call(n, child_values)
          end
          @values[@node]
        end

        private
          def traverse_bottom_up(node, &block)
            call_stack, processing_stack = [ node ], []

            until call_stack.empty?
              node = call_stack.pop
              processing_stack.push(node)
              call_stack.concat node.children
            end

            processing_stack.reverse_each(&block)
          end
      end
  end
end
"
}

messages.thinking:
**Deconstructing the Bot Mention Removal Logic**

Okay, here's the breakdown, as I see it. This is about stripping a bot's own @-mention from a message body, the goal is to get clean, usable text. I need to be *sure* I'm not mangling the message in the process.

Let's start with the basic idea: create a unique sentinel string and insert it in place of the bot's mention. The logic then becomes about effectively *removing* that sentinel and any surrounding whitespace, while handling a variety of edge cases.

I'm thinking, `plain_text_without_mention_of(bot)` seems like a good method name, or maybe `plain_text_for_bot(bot)`.

The sentinel itself, a unique string like `"\uFFFC__BOT_MENTION__#{SecureRandom.hex(8)}\uFFFC"`, is crucial. Let's compare this sentinel approach to potential DOM manipulations to see which is more robust.

Now, let's step through the logic.

1.  We start with the message body (`message.body.body`), handling a `nil` case.
2.  `content.render_attachments` inserts the sentinel, replacing instances of the bot with the sentinel.
3.  We convert this to plain text: `plain = rendered.fragment.to_plain_text`

The real work is in the *removal* of the sentinel string. Let's map how `plain` will behave in a few cases:

*   **Case 1:** `"@Bot restart the build please"` - `plain` becomes something like `#{sentinel} restart the build please`. We need to handle the leading space.
*   **Case 2:** `"restart the build please @Bot "` - `plain` is `"restart the build please #{sentinel} "`. Trailing space again!
*   **Case 3:** `"please @Bot restart the build"` - `plain` will be `"please #{sentinel} restart the build"`. This one is interesting; it's got space before *and* after. This means `/([ \t\u00a0])#{Regexp.escape(sentinel)}[ \t\u00a0]+/` and replacing with `'\1'` will collapse both spaces into one! That is good!
*   **Case 4:** Multiple mentions at the start: `"@Bot @OtherBot deploy"`. The process needs to iterate to strip multiple mentions.
*   **Case 5:** Just the bot mention: `"@Bot"` or `"@Bot "` should result in an empty string. The logic has to collapse those spaces!
*   **Case 6:** Newline immediately after the mention: `"@Bot\nrestart the build"` - We can just strip the leading/trailing whitespace after removing.
*   **Case 7:** Punctuation right after the mention: `"@Bot, restart the build"` - This is where we *have* to be careful! We *never* strip punctuation!  The best approach is to only remove the mention and any adjacent spaces.
*   **Case 8:** Multiple mentions of the *same* bot: `"@Bot hey @Bot restart"` - We'll need a combination of regex patterns to handle this: at the start, between spaces, and the end.
*   **Case 9:** Multiple mentions of the *same* bot right *next* to each other: `"@Bot @Bot restart"` - If using a loop with the regex or a non-greedy expression, this collapses to the desired result.

I need to make sure that the regex only strips the mention and adjacent space, never any punctuation. Otherwise, commands with punctuation like `@Bot /status` would break, which is unacceptable.

Okay, I've got a good handle on the edge cases. Let's test all these with a Rails runner and verify the behavior!

**Implementation Plan: Webhook Delivery for Bots** Okay, let's break this down. We're building webhook functionality for our bots. First, we need to ensure the `webhook_url` is cleared when a bot is deactivated in `app/models/user.rb`. Then, we have the core bot model in `app/models/user/bot.rb`. We'll need to handle URL normalization, scope bots with webhooks, validate the URL, and then the critical pieces: queuing webhook delivery later, and actually *delivering* the webhook when needed. The associated webhook logic itself will be encapsulated in `app/models/user/bot/webhook.rb`. That webhook class is where the action is: crafting the payload, making the `Net::HTTP` POST request (crucially, we must handle the request and response *together*), setting the right `Content-Type`, handling both `200` and `204` responses. We'll also need to carefully handle UTF-8 decoding of the response body. If the response is good, then we broadcast a create message. For asynchronous delivery, `app/jobs/bots/webhook_delivery_job.rb` will be used. Then we'll need `app/models/message/mentionee.rb` to correctly handle the mentions of these bots. `app/models/room.rb` will be updated to kick off webhook delivery on message receipt. We will create a controller to manage the Bots, and within this a messages controller to handle the different content types. The UI will need an update with a form for the webhook URL. Now, let's *really* dig into the details. I'm going to start with `app/models/user/bot/webhook.rb`. I need to be absolutely certain we handle the `Net::HTTP` interaction correctly. The most important part of this is the request to the webhook endpoint, and how we handle the response body. The `OPEN_TIMEOUT`, `READ_TIMEOUT`, and `WRITE_TIMEOUT` constants are important, as is the maximum response size. I'm focusing on that `post_json` method. I'm going to set up the request and the options for the HTTP request. We have to make sure we set the content type to `application/json` and that we correctly serialize the payload to JSON. And then *how* we make that HTTP call is crucial. I need to use `Net::HTTP.start` to make the request, but I need to call `http.request(request)` with a block. This lets me read the response. Then, inside the block, I have to call `read_limited_body`. The `read_limited_body` method is very important, because it handles chunking the response body. We read in chunks, and if we hit the limit, we return nil, so the caller doesn't try to parse too much data. We want to avoid a situation where a malicious webhook can send a very large response and cause our server to run out of memory. Here's the key: if we call `response.read_body` inside the `Net::HTTP.start` block, we can't access `response.body` *later* unless we pass the *response* and the read *body* as a pair! We need to ensure that the method `post_json` *returns* or *yields* both the `response` *and* the read `body`. This avoids that tricky `IOError` from trying to read the body twice. And this clean signature - `[ response, body ]` - is perfect. Let's look at `read_limited_body`. First, we handle the case where the response is a `204 No Content` which indicates we return an empty string. Otherwise, we're going to read chunks of the response body, and if the total size exceeds `MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE` we return `nil`. Now, how will `handle_response` use the `response` and the `body`? We check if the response code is 200, and if there is a non-empty body. Then, we decode it. The `decode_body` method is responsible for detecting the charset of the response body, and for converting the body to UTF-8. require "test_helper"

class User::BotTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "creating a bot generates a unique bot_key and joins open rooms" do
    Current.user = users(:kevin)

    bot = nil
    assert_difference -> { Membership.count }, +Rooms::Open.count do
      bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")
    end

    assert bot.bot?
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert bot.bot_token.present?
    assert_equal "#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}", bot.bot_key
    assert_nil bot.webhook_url
    assert_not bot.webhook_configured?
    assert_not bot.can_administer?
    assert_equal Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).sort, bot.rooms.pluck(:id).sort
  end

  test "bot accepts optional http or https webhook_url including localhost and clears blank values" do
    bot = User.bot.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin), webhook_url: "  http://localhost:4567/webhook?env=test  ")
    assert_equal "http://localhost:4567/webhook?env=test", bot.webhook_url
    assert bot.webhook_configured?

    bot.update!(webhook_url: "https://127.0.0.1:8443/hook")
    assert_equal "https://127.0.0.1:8443/hook", bot.webhook_url

    bot.update!(webhook_url: "   ")
    assert_nil bot.reload.webhook_url
    assert_not bot.webhook_configured?
  end

  test "bot rejects invalid webhook_url" do
    [ "not-a-url", "ftp://example.com/hook", "javascript:alert(1)", "http://" ].each do |invalid_url|
      bot = User.new(role: :bot, name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin), webhook_url: invalid_url)
      assert_not bot.valid?, "Expected #{invalid_url.inspect} to be invalid"
      assert_includes bot.errors[:webhook_url], "is invalid"
    end
  end

  test "human users do not get a bot_token, bot_key, or webhook_url" do
    user = User.create!(name: "Human", email_address: "human@example.com", password: "secret123456", webhook_url: "https://example.com/hook")

    assert_not user.bot?
    assert_nil user.bot_token
    assert_nil user.bot_key
    assert_nil user.webhook_url
  end

  test "bot requires a name" do
    bot = User.new(role: :bot, name: "   ", creator: users(:kevin))

    assert_not bot.valid?\
    assert_includes bot.errors[:name], "can't be blank"
  end

  test "authenticate_bot validates bot_key securely" do
    bot = User.bot.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin))

    assert_equal bot, User.authenticate_bot(bot.bot_key)
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}-wrongtoken")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("0#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}x-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("999999-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{users(:david).id}-anything")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("-")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(nil)
  end

    bot = User.bot.create!(name: "Deploy Bot", creator: users(:kevin), webhook_url: "https://example.com/webhook")

cat <<'EOF' > docs/bots.md ## Chat Bots Architecture & Design Notes ### Data Model Bots are modeled as `User` records (`role: :bot`, see `app/models/user/bot.rb` and `app/models/user/role.rb`): - **`users.role`**: `enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]` (`2` = `bot`). - **`users.bot_token`**: 24-character base58 random credential generated via `generate_unique_secure_token` on creation (`nil` for human users and cleared to `nil` when a bot is deactivated). - **`users.webhook_url`**: nullable HTTP/HTTPS callback URL normalized via `strip.presence` (`nil` for human users, cleared to `nil` when saved empty or when a bot is deactivated). - **`users.creator_id`**: nullable self-referential foreign key (`on_delete: :nullify`) tracking which chat member created the bot. - **`users.password_digest`**: nullable so bots cannot authenticate via password/session login. Modeling bots on `User` means bots reuse existing `Membership`, `Room`, `Message` (`creator_id` FK to `users`), `User::Avatar`, `User::Mentionable`, `Message::Broadcasts`, and `Room::MessagePusher` pipelines without polymorphism or schema duplication: - **Open rooms**: `User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (`after_create_commit`) and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users` include active bots automatically. - **Closed & direct rooms**: `Rooms::ClosedsController`, `Rooms::DirectsController`, and `Autocompletable::UsersController` query `User.active`, allowing bots to be added to rooms and `@-mentioned` in autocomplete the same way as people. - **Human-only surfaces**: `User.without_bots` excludes bots from the `/account/edit` member management list, session login/transfer, IP bans, and direct-message sidebar placeholders. - **Soft deletion**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, setting `status: :deactivated`, clearing `bot_token: nil` and `webhook_url: nil`, and removing non-direct room memberships while keeping historical messages authored by the bot intact. ### Ownership & Authorization - Any signed-in member can access `/bots`, `/bots/new`, and `POST /bots`. - `/bots` (`BotsController#index`) lists `Current.user.bots.active` for regular members and `User.active_bots` for administrators on a single page without pagination, with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `turbo-cache-control: no-store`. - `User::Role#can_administer?(record)` returns `false` for bots themselves, `true` for administrators, and `true` when `self == record&.creator`, authorizing `edit`, `update`, and `destroy` on `BotsController`. ### Bot Code & HTTP Messaging API - **Bot code format**: `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"` (`User#bot_key`). `User.authenticate_bot` verifies numeric `id`, active bot status, and compares the full `bot_key` via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`. - **Log hygiene**: `:bot_code` (alongside `:token` and `:_key`) is filtered in `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb`. - **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`Bots::MessagesController#create`). - Inherits from `ActionController::Base` (including `ActiveStorage::SetCurrent`, `BlockBannedRequests`, `SetCurrentRequest`, `VersionHeaders`) so CLI User-Agents are never blocked by browser version gates. - Overrides `self.dispatch` for non-multipart requests to set `action_dispatch.request.request_parameters = {}` so raw shell payloads sent via `curl -d "..."` (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) containing `%`, `&`, or arbitrary bytes never trigger `ActionController::BadRequest` before reaching the action, and raw message text is kept out of parameter logs. - Reads `request.raw_post` as UTF-8: HTML-escapes plain/form bodies and converts newlines to `

I have implemented bot webhooks for @-mentions in Campfire:

- **Webhook URL Configuration (`User::Bot`, `BotsController`, `app/views/bots/_form.html.erb`, `db/migrate/20251214000000_add_webhook_url_to_users.rb`)**:
  - Added an optional `webhook_url` attribute to bots (`users.webhook_url`) normalized via `strip.presence`, validated as a valid HTTP/HTTPS URL, and cleared when saved empty or when a bot is deactivated.
  - Added the optional `"Webhook URL"` field (with both `<label>` text and `placeholder="Webhook URL"`) to the shared bot form used by `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit`.
- **@-Mention Autocomplete & Asynchronous Webhook Triggering (`Autocompletable::UsersController`, `Message::Mentionee`, `Room#receive`, `Bots::WebhookDeliveryJob`)**:
  - Active bots appear in room `@-mention` autocomplete alongside human members.
  - Mentioning a bot in a room it belongs to enqueues `Bots::WebhookDeliveryJob` on the `default` queue so slow or failing webhooks never block message posting. Bot-authored messages never trigger webhooks to prevent loops.
- **Payload & Synchronous / Asynchronous Replies (`User::Bot::Webhook`, `Bots::MessagesController`)**:
  - Sends a `POST` request with `Content-Type: application/json` containing `event` (`"mention"`), `author` (`{ id, name }`), `room` (`{ id, name, reply_to }`), and `message` (`{ id, body: { text, html }, link }`) with the bot's own `@-mention` stripped from `body.text` and relative paths for `reply_to` and `link`.
  - Handles `200` responses with `Content-Type: text/plain` or `text/html` by posting and broadcasting the response body into the room as the bot's message, and ignores `204` responses so bots can reply asynchronously via `room.reply_to` or remain silent.
- **Documentation & Tests**:
  - Documented the webhook design in `docs/bots.md` and added unit, controller, integration, and real-socket tests.
